guide:
# pyi-thon

Thirty levels, three phases. Each mission is one small Python program. Check runs your code in a local sandbox and compares the printed output.

When a mission says it is reading input, the game feeds the sample input for you. You still call input().

The reference answer stays hidden until you ask for it. Hints start with the idea, not the whole program.

modules.name: pythonic
modules.blurb: Comprehensions, f-strings, and a last filter.

levels.title: Hello, World!
levels.objective:
Use print() to display exactly: Hello, World!

The print() function outputs text to the screen. Text must be wrapped in quotes.
hints: The print() function outputs text to the screen. Text must be wrapped in quotes.
Use print() to display exactly: Hello, World!
Shape of the program: Remember: print("text goes here")
levels.debrief: print() is Python's built-in function for displaying output. Strings (text) must be wrapped in quotes - single or double.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.
levels.answer: print("Hello, World!")

levels.title: Variables & Assignment
levels.objective:
Create a variable called name set to "Alice", then print it.

Variables store data. Use = to assign a value. Python figures out the type automatically.
hints: Variables store data. Use = to assign a value. Python figures out the type automatically.
Create a variable called name set to "Alice", then print it.
Shape of the program: Two lines: assign the variable, then print(variable_name)
levels.debrief: Variables are like labeled boxes. name = "Alice" creates a box labeled "name" containing the text "Alice".
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.
levels.answer:
name = "Alice"
print(name)
levels.scaffold: # Create a variable and print it

guards.message: Create a variable called name.
Print the variable, not a hardcoded string.

levels.title: String Concatenation
levels.objective:
Create name = "Alice" and age = 25, then print: "Alice is 25"

The + operator joins strings together. Numbers must be converted with str() first.
hints: The + operator joins strings together. Numbers must be converted with str() first.
Create name = "Alice" and age = 25, then print: "Alice is 25"
Shape of the program: Use + to join strings. Remember str(age) to convert the integer!
levels.debrief: Strings and integers can't be directly concatenated. str() converts a number to a string so + can join them.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.
levels.answer:
name = "Alice"
age = 25
print(name + " is " + str(age))

guards.message: Use str(), an f-string, or format() to combine the text and the number.

levels.title: User Input
levels.objective:
Write code that asks "What is your name? " and prints: Hello, <name>

input() pauses the program and waits for the user to type something. It always returns a string.
hints: input() pauses the program and waits for the user to type something. It always returns a string.
Write code that asks "What is your name? " and prints: Hello, <name>
Shape of the program: name = input("question") then print("Hello, " + name)
levels.debrief: input("prompt") displays the prompt and waits. The returned value is always a string.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.
levels.answer:
name = input("What is your name? ")
print("Hello, " + name)
levels.scaffold: # Ask for input and greet the user

guards.message: Use input() to ask for the name.

levels.title: If/Else Logic
levels.objective:
Set score = 85. If score >= 70, print "pass". Otherwise print "fail".

if checks a condition. If True, the indented block runs. else runs when the condition is False.
hints: if checks a condition. If True, the indented block runs. else runs when the condition is False.
Set score = 85. If score >= 70, print "pass". Otherwise print "fail".

Shape of the program: if score >= 70:
    print(...)
else:
    print(...)
levels.debrief: if/else creates a branch - the program takes one path or the other based on the condition.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.
levels.scaffold:
# Check if the score is passing
score = 85

guards.message: Use both if and else.

levels.title: Elif Chains
levels.objective:
Set grade = 82. Print "A" if >= 90, "B" if >= 80, "C" if >= 70, else "F".

elif (else-if) lets you check additional conditions. Python checks top to bottom and runs the FIRST match.
hints: elif (else-if) lets you check additional conditions. Python checks top to bottom and runs the FIRST match.
Set grade = 82. Print "A" if >= 90, "B" if >= 80, "C" if >= 70, else "F".

Shape of the program: if grade >= 90:
    ...
elif grade >= 80:
    ...
elif ...
levels.debrief: elif chains check conditions in order. Once a match is found, the rest are skipped.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.

guards.message: Use elif for the extra conditions.

levels.title: For Loops
levels.objective:
Print the numbers 0 through 4, each on a new line.

for i in range(n) repeats a block n times. i starts at 0 and goes to n-1.
hints: for i in range(n) repeats a block n times. i starts at 0 and goes to n-1.
Print the numbers 0 through 4, each on a new line.
Shape of the program: for i in range(5):\n    print(i)
levels.debrief: range(5) generates 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.
levels.answer:
for i in range(5):
    print(i)

guards.message: Use a for loop with range().

levels.title: While Loops
levels.objective:
Use a while loop to print numbers 1 through 5.

while condition: keeps looping as long as the condition is True. You must change the condition inside!
hints: while condition: keeps looping as long as the condition is True. You must change the condition inside!
Use a while loop to print numbers 1 through 5.

Shape of the program: count = 1
while count <= 5:
    print(count)
    count = count + 1
levels.debrief: While loops check their condition before each iteration.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.
levels.guide: Looping until a condition is false
levels.answer:
count = 1
while count <= 5:
    print(count)
    count = count + 1

guards.message: Use a while loop.

levels.title: Interactive Loop
levels.objective:
Ask the user for a number 3 times and print each one.

You can use input() inside a while loop to repeatedly ask the user for data.
hints: You can use input() inside a while loop to repeatedly ask the user for data.
Ask the user for a number 3 times and print each one.

Shape of the program: count = 0
while count < 3:
    num = input(...)
    print(num)
    count = count + 1
levels.debrief: Combining loops with input() creates interactive programs.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.
levels.answer:
count = 0
while count < 3:
    num = input()
    print(num)
    count = count + 1

guards.message: Use a while loop and input().

levels.title: Running Total
levels.objective:
Calculate the sum of numbers 1 through 5 using a loop. Print the total.

Start a variable at 0 before the loop. Add to it each iteration. This is the accumulator pattern.
hints: Start a variable at 0 before the loop. Add to it each iteration. This is the accumulator pattern.
Calculate the sum of numbers 1 through 5 using a loop. Print the total.

Shape of the program: total = 0
for i in range(1, 6):
    total = total + i
print(total)
levels.debrief: The accumulator pattern: (1) initialize total = 0, (2) loop and add, (3) use total after the loop.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.
levels.answer:
total = 0
for i in range(1, 6):
    total = total + i
print(total)

guards.message: Use a loop to add the numbers up.

levels.title: Averages
levels.objective:
Calculate the average of 10, 20, and 30. Print the result.

Average = total / count. The / operator returns a float (decimal).
hints: Average = total / count. The / operator returns a float (decimal).
Calculate the average of 10, 20, and 30. Print the result.
Shape of the program: total = 10 + 20 + 30\naverage = total / 3\nprint(average)
levels.debrief: / always returns a float in Python 3 (20.0 not 20).
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.
levels.answer:
total = 10 + 20 + 30
average = total / 3
print(average)

guards.message: Use / to divide.

levels.title: Sentinel Loop
levels.objective:
Read numbers from input until "done" is typed. Print the sum. Inputs: 5, 10, 15, done.

A sentinel loop runs until the user types a special keyword (like "done") to stop.
hints: A sentinel loop runs until the user types a special keyword (like "done") to stop.
Read numbers from input until "done" is typed. Print the sum. Inputs: 5, 10, 15, done.

Shape of the program: total = 0
while True:
    val = input(...)
    if val == "done":
        break
    total = total + int(val)
print(total)
levels.debrief: "while True" + "break" is the sentinel pattern.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.
levels.answer:
total = 0
while True:
    val = input()
    if val == "done":
        break
    total = total + int(val)
print(total)

guards.message: Use a while loop.
Use break to stop when the input is done.
Use input() to read each value.

levels.title: Functions: def & return
levels.objective:
Write a function called double that takes a number and returns it times 2. Print double(7).

def creates a function. return sends a value back.
hints: def creates a function. return sends a value back.
Write a function called double that takes a number and returns it times 2. Print double(7).
Shape of the program: def double(n):\n    return n * 2\nprint(double(7))
levels.debrief: "def" defines, parameters go in parentheses, "return" sends back the result.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.

guards.message: Define a function and return the value.

levels.title: Multiple Parameters
levels.objective:
Write greet(name, greeting) that returns greeting + ", " + name. Print greet("Alice", "Hello").

Functions can accept multiple parameters, separated by commas.
hints: Functions can accept multiple parameters, separated by commas.
Write greet(name, greeting) that returns greeting + ", " + name. Print greet("Alice", "Hello").
Shape of the program: def greet(name, greeting):\n    return greeting + ", " + name
levels.debrief: Parameters are variable names in the definition. Arguments are the actual values you pass in.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.

guards.message: Define greet(...) and return the greeting.

levels.title: Lists: Create & Access
levels.objective:
Create fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]. Print the second item.

Lists hold multiple values in order. Access items by index starting at 0.
hints: Lists hold multiple values in order. Access items by index starting at 0.
Create fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]. Print the second item.
Shape of the program: Index 0 is the first, index 1 is the second.
levels.debrief: Lists are indexed starting at 0.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.
levels.answer:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
print(fruits[1])
levels.scaffold: # Create a list and access an item

guards.message: Create a list with square brackets.

levels.title: List Methods
levels.objective:
Start with nums = [1, 2, 3]. Append 4, then print the length.

.append(item) adds to the end. len() returns length.
hints: .append(item) adds to the end. len() returns length.
Start with nums = [1, 2, 3]. Append 4, then print the length.
Shape of the program: nums.append(4)\nprint(len(nums))
levels.debrief: .append() modifies the list in-place. len() is a built-in.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.
levels.answer:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
nums.append(4)
print(len(nums))

guards.message: Use .append() and len().

levels.title: Dictionaries
levels.objective:
Create person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 25}. Print person["name"].

Dicts store key: value pairs inside {}. Access values by key name.
hints: Dicts store key: value pairs inside {}. Access values by key name.
Create person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 25}. Print person["name"].
Shape of the program: Use curly braces and "key": value syntax.
levels.debrief: Dicts map keys to values. JSON is essentially nested dictionaries.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.
levels.answer:
person = {"name": "Alice", "age": 25}
print(person["name"])

guards.message: Create a dictionary with { } or dict().

levels.title: Looping Through a Dict
levels.objective:
Create scores = {"math": 90, "science": 85}. Loop and print each like: math: 90

.items() returns key-value pairs you can loop over.
hints: .items() returns key-value pairs you can loop over.
Create scores = {"math": 90, "science": 85}. Loop and print each like: math: 90
Shape of the program: for subject, score in scores.items():\n    print(subject + ": " + str(score))
levels.debrief: .items() unpacks each pair into two variables.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.

guards.message: Loop with for and .items().

levels.title: Mini App: To-Do List
levels.objective:
Build a to-do app: create a list, loop to ask for tasks, append until "done", then print all tasks.

A real program combines lists, loops, input, and functions.
hints: A real program combines lists, loops, input, and functions.
Build a to-do app: create a list, loop to ask for tasks, append until "done", then print all tasks.
levels.debrief: Combines sentinel loops, lists, append, and iteration.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.

guards.message: Use a while loop, input(), and .append().

levels.title: File I/O: Writing
levels.objective:
Write "Hello from Python" to output.txt, then read it back and print the contents.

open("file", "w") creates/overwrites a file. Use "with" to auto-close.
hints: open("file", "w") creates/overwrites a file. Use "with" to auto-close.
Write "Hello from Python" to output.txt, then read it back and print the contents.

Shape of the program: with open("output.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write(...)
with open("output.txt", "r") as f:
    print(f.read())
levels.debrief: "with" handles opening AND closing the file automatically.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.
levels.answer:
with open("output.txt", "w") as handle:
    handle.write("Hello from Python")
with open("output.txt") as handle:
    print(handle.read())
levels.scaffold: # Write to a file, then read it

guards.message: Use open() to write and read the file.

levels.title: Try/Except
levels.objective:
Try to convert "hello" to int. Catch the ValueError and print "Not a number".

try/except catches errors so your program doesn't crash.
hints: try/except catches errors so your program doesn't crash.
Try to convert "hello" to int. Catch the ValueError and print "Not a number".

Shape of the program: try:
    int("hello")
except ValueError:
    print("Not a number")
levels.debrief: try/except wraps risky operations so errors are handled gracefully.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.

guards.message: Use try and except.

levels.title: Classes: Basics
levels.objective:
Create class Dog with __init__(self, name) and bark() returning name + " says woof!". Print Dog("Rex").bark().

A class is a blueprint for objects. __init__ runs on creation. self refers to the instance.
hints: A class is a blueprint for objects. __init__ runs on creation. self refers to the instance.
Create class Dog with __init__(self, name) and bark() returning name + " says woof!". Print Dog("Rex").bark().
levels.debrief: Classes organize code - __init__ for setup, methods for behavior.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.

guards.message: Write a class with __init__ and self.

levels.title: Working with JSON
levels.objective:
Import json. Create data = {"app": "MyApp", "version": 2}. Convert to JSON string and back, then print data["app"].

The json module converts between JSON strings and Python dictionaries.
hints: The json module converts between JSON strings and Python dictionaries.
Import json. Create data = {"app": "MyApp", "version": 2}. Convert to JSON string and back, then print data["app"].

Shape of the program: import json
data = {...}
json_str = json.dumps(data)
parsed = json.loads(json_str)
print(parsed["app"])
levels.debrief: json.dumps() = dict to string. json.loads() = string to dict.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.
levels.answer:
import json
data = {"app": "MyApp", "version": 2}
json_str = json.dumps(data)
parsed = json.loads(json_str)
print(parsed["app"])

guards.message: Import json, then use dumps and loads.

levels.title: Import & Structure
levels.objective:
Import math, define circle_area(r) returning math.pi * r * r, print rounded to 2 decimals for r=5.

Real Python files follow a pattern: imports at top, then definitions, then execution.
hints: Real Python files follow a pattern: imports at top, then definitions, then execution.
Import math, define circle_area(r) returning math.pi * r * r, print rounded to 2 decimals for r=5.

Shape of the program: import math
def circle_area(r):
    return math.pi * r * r
print(round(circle_area(5), 2))
levels.debrief: The standard pattern: imports at top, function definitions, then execution code.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.
levels.answer:
import math
def circle_area(r):
    return math.pi * r * r
print(round(circle_area(5), 2))

guards.message: Import math, define a function, and use math.pi.

levels.title: Graduation: Score Tracker
levels.objective:
Create scores = {"python": 85, "git": 90}. Write get_average(scores_dict) to return the average. Print rounded to 1 decimal.

This graduation exercise ties together dicts, functions, and built-in operations.
hints: This graduation exercise ties together dicts, functions, and built-in operations.
Create scores = {"python": 85, "git": 90}. Write get_average(scores_dict) to return the average. Print rounded to 1 decimal.
levels.debrief: Combines dicts, built-ins (sum, len, round), and custom functions.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.

guards.message: Define a function that uses sum() and len().

levels.title: List Comprehensions
levels.objective:
Create a list of squares for 1-5 using a list comprehension. Print it.

[expression for item in iterable] creates a new list in one line.
hints: [expression for item in iterable] creates a new list in one line.
Create a list of squares for 1-5 using a list comprehension. Print it.
Shape of the program: squares = [x * x for x in range(1, 6)]\nprint(squares)
levels.debrief: List comprehensions replace 4 lines of loop code with 1 elegant line.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.
levels.answer:
squares = [x * x for x in range(1, 6)]
print(squares)

guards.message: Use a list comprehension: [expr for x in iterable].

levels.title: String Methods
levels.objective:
Set text = "hello world python". Split by spaces, join with hyphens, and print the result.

Strings have powerful built-in methods for manipulation.
hints: Strings have powerful built-in methods for manipulation.
Set text = "hello world python". Split by spaces, join with hyphens, and print the result.
Shape of the program: words = text.split(" ")\nresult = "-".join(words)\nprint(result)
levels.debrief: .split() breaks a string into a list. .join() combines a list back into a string.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.
levels.answer:
text = "hello world python"
print("-".join(text.split(" ")))

guards.message: Use .split() and .join().

levels.title: F-Strings
levels.objective:
Set language = "Python" and version = 3. Print: "Python version 3 is awesome!"

f"...{variable}..." embeds variables directly in strings. Much cleaner than concatenation.
hints: f"...{variable}..." embeds variables directly in strings. Much cleaner than concatenation.
Set language = "Python" and version = 3. Print: "Python version 3 is awesome!"
Shape of the program: print(f"{language} version {version} is awesome!")
levels.debrief: F-strings (Python 3.6+) are the modern, preferred way to format strings.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.
levels.answer:
language = "Python"
version = 3
print(f"{language} version {version} is awesome!")

guards.message: Use an f-string.

levels.title: Lambda & Map
levels.objective:
Use map with a lambda to triple every number in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Print the resulting list.

lambda creates small anonymous functions. map() applies a function to every item in a list.
hints: lambda creates small anonymous functions. map() applies a function to every item in a list.
Use map with a lambda to triple every number in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Print the resulting list.
Shape of the program: result = list(map(lambda x: x * 3, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]))\nprint(result)
levels.debrief: lambda x: x * 3 is a compact one-line function.
levels.mistakes: Match the text exactly, including spaces and capitalization. If the mission uses input(), call input() instead of hardcoding the sample.
levels.answer:
result = list(map(lambda x: x * 3, [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]))
print(result)

guards.message: Use lambda and map().

levels.objective:
Given a list of student dicts (name/score), print only the names of students with scores >= 80.

Real programs follow a pattern: parse input, transform data, produce output.
hints: Real programs follow a pattern: parse input, transform data, produce output.
Given a list of student dicts (name/score), print only the names of students with scores >= 80.
Shape of the program: for s in students:\n    if s["score"] >= 80:\n        print(s["name"])
